claim: Projections from the basal amygdala (BA) to the ventral hippocampus (vH) are proposed to provide information about the rewarding or threatening nature of learned associations to support appropriate goal-directed and anxiety-like behaviour.
source: Projections from the basal amygdala (BA) to the ventral hippocampus (vH) are proposed to provide information about the rewarding or threatening nature of learned associations to support appropriate goal-directed and anxiety-like behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: BA input to vH consists of both excitatory and inhibitory projections.
source: Using channelrhodopsin-2-assisted circuit mapping in mice, we show that BA input to vH consists of both excitatory and inhibitory projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from channelrhodopsin-2-assisted circuit mapping shown in Figure 2.

claim: Excitatory input from BA specifically targets BA- and nucleus accumbens-projecting vH neurons.
source: Excitatory input specifically targets BA- and nucleus accumbens-projecting vH neurons and avoids prefrontal cortex-projecting vH neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiology recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Excitatory input from BA avoids prefrontal cortex-projecting vH neurons.
source: Excitatory input specifically targets BA- and nucleus accumbens-projecting vH neurons and avoids prefrontal cortex-projecting vH neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiology recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Inhibitory input from BA preferentially targets BA-projecting neurons.
source: while inhibitory input preferentially targets BA-projecting neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired electrophysiology recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: BA inhibitory projections gate place-value associations by controlling the activity of nucleus accumbens-projecting vH neurons.
source: Through this specific connectivity, BA inhibitory projections gate place-value associations by controlling the activity of nucleus accumbens-projecting vH neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo optogenetics and pharmacology experiments shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The hippocampus is key for episodic memory, learning and spatial navigation, as well as motivation, affect and anxiety.
source: The hippocampus is key for episodic memory, learning and spatial navigation, as well as motivation, affect and anxiety (Gray and McNaughton, 2003; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Strange et al., 2014; Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The hippocampus is organised as a gradient along the dorsal to ventral axis.
source: At almost every level of investigation – from gene expression, to afferent and efferent connectivity, and behavioural function – the hippocampus is organised as a gradient along the dorsal to ventral (posterior to anterior in humans) axis (Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The most dorsal portion of the hippocampus is proposed to be involved in learning and utilising fine-grained spatial and temporal structure.
source: Within this axis the most dorsal portion is proposed to be involved in learning and utilising fine-grained spatial and temporal structure, whereas the most ventral pole is thought to be involved in affect and motivation, and has a key role in value-based and reward-driven decision-making and anxiety-like calculations (Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The most ventral pole of the hippocampus is thought to be involved in affect and motivation, and has a key role in value-based and reward-driven decision-making and anxiety-like calculations.
source: Within this axis the most dorsal portion is proposed to be involved in learning and utilising fine-grained spatial and temporal structure, whereas the most ventral pole is thought to be involved in affect and motivation, and has a key role in value-based and reward-driven decision-making and anxiety-like calculations (Fanselow and Dong, 2010; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ventral hippocampus receives dense input from the corticobasolateral nuclear complex of the amygdala.
source: A distinguishing factor that separates the ventral from the dorsal hippocampus is dense input from the corticobasolateral nuclear complex of the amygdala (basal amygdala [BA]; McDonald and Mott, 2017; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The BA comprises a diverse set of nuclei including the basolateral amygdala (BLA), the basomedial amygdala (BMA), the medial amygdala (MEA) and cortical amygdala.
source: The BA comprises a diverse set of nuclei including the basolateral amygdala (BLA), the basomedial amygdala (BMA), the medial amygdala (MEA) and cortical amygdala, each of which sends projections to ventral hippocampus (vH) (McDonald and Mott, 2017; Petrovich et al., 2001; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each BA nucleus sends projections to ventral hippocampus.
source: The BA comprises a diverse set of nuclei including the basolateral amygdala (BLA), the basomedial amygdala (BMA), the medial amygdala (MEA) and cortical amygdala, each of which sends projections to ventral hippocampus (vH) (McDonald and Mott, 2017; Petrovich et al., 2001; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BA nuclei and their projections to vH are thought to be crucial for the learning of reward- and threat-associated cues, and for the generation of appropriate goal-directed and anxiety-like behaviour.
source: These nuclei, and their projections to vH, are thought to be crucial for the learning of reward- and threat-associated cues, and for the generation of appropriate goal-directed and anxiety-like behaviour (Beyeler et al., 2018; Beyeler et al., 2016; Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014; Hitchcott and Phillips, 1997; McHugh et al., 2004; Pi et al., 2020; Richardson et al., 2004; Selden et al., 1991; Sheth et al., 2008; Yang and Wang, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: There is limited information describing the organisation of functional connectivity between amygdala input and neurons in vH.
source: However, there is limited information describing the organisation of such functional connectivity between amygdala input and neurons in vH (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a gap in knowledge.

claim: The majority of neurons in vH project to only one downstream area.
source: This lack of understanding is compounded by the fact that the vH, in particular its output structure the ventral CA1 and subiculum – where the majority of BA input is found – is organised as a parallel circuit, such that the majority of neurons project to only one downstream area (Gergues et al., 2020; Naber and Witter, 1998; Wee and MacAskill, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vH has powerful connections to the nucleus accumbens (NAc), the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and back to the BA, each arising from a distinct population of neurons.
source: Thus, while vH has powerful connections to the nucleus accumbens (NAc), the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and back to the BA, each of these projections arises from a distinct population of neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each vH projection population is increasingly shown to underlie unique behavioural functions.
source: Importantly each of these projection populations is increasingly shown to underlie unique behavioural functions (Adhikari et al., 2010; Jimenez et al., 2018; LeGates et al., 2018; Sanchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vHNAc neuron activity is high during motivated behaviour and around rewarded locations.
source: For example, vHNAc neuron activity is high during motivated behaviour and around rewarded locations (Ciocchi et al., 2015; Okuyama et al., 2016; Reed et al., 2018), is necessary for place-value associations (LeGates et al., 2018; Trouche et al., 2019) and can promote spatial and instrumental reinforcement (Britt et al., 2012; LeGates et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vHNAc neuron activity is necessary for place-value associations.
source: For example, vHNAc neuron activity is high during motivated behaviour and around rewarded locations (Ciocchi et al., 2015; Okuyama et al., 2016; Reed et al., 2018), is necessary for place-value associations (LeGates et al., 2018; Trouche et al., 2019) and can promote spatial and instrumental reinforcement (Britt et al., 2012; LeGates et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vHNAc neuron activity can promote spatial and instrumental reinforcement.
source: For example, vHNAc neuron activity is high during motivated behaviour and around rewarded locations (Ciocchi et al., 2015; Okuyama et al., 2016; Reed et al., 2018), is necessary for place-value associations (LeGates et al., 2018; Trouche et al., 2019) and can promote spatial and instrumental reinforcement (Britt et al., 2012; LeGates et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vHPFC activity is proposed to support the resolution of approach avoidance conflict and contribute to spatial working memory.
source: In contrast, vHPFC activity is proposed to support the resolution of approach avoidance conflict and contribute to spatial working memory (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Sanchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2021; Spellman et al., 2015), while vHBA activity is proposed to support contextual learning (Jimenez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vHBA activity is proposed to support contextual learning.
source: In contrast, vHPFC activity is proposed to support the resolution of approach avoidance conflict and contribute to spatial working memory (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Sanchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2021; Spellman et al., 2015), while vHBA activity is proposed to support contextual learning (Jimenez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The majority of neurons in BA are classed as either excitatory pyramidal neurons or local inhibitory interneurons.
source: The circuit organisation of the nuclei in the BA is similar to classic cortical circuitry – with the majority of neurons classed as either excitatory pyramidal neurons or local inhibitory interneurons (McDonald and Mott, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is evidence suggesting the presence of long-range inhibitory projection neurons throughout BA.
source: However, there is also evidence suggesting the presence of long-range inhibitory projection neurons throughout BA (Dedic et al., 2018; McDonald et al., 2012; McDonald and Zaric, 2015; Seo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Long-range inhibitory projections from cortex are hypothesised to have a crucial regulatory role in modulating hippocampal circuit function.
source: Similar inhibitory projections from cortex are hypothesised to have a crucial regulatory role in modulating hippocampal circuit function (Basu et al., 2016; Melzer et al., 2012), but the connectivity and function of BA long-range inhibitory input in vH has never been directly investigated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The connectivity and function of BA long-range inhibitory input in vH has never been directly investigated.
source: Similar inhibitory projections from cortex are hypothesised to have a crucial regulatory role in modulating hippocampal circuit function (Basu et al., 2016; Melzer et al., 2012), but the connectivity and function of BA long-range inhibitory input in vH has never been directly investigated.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge identified by the authors.

claim: Neurons sending input to vH were widely dispersed throughout the entire BA, including in BLA, BMA and MEA, as well as in more cortical amygdala areas.
source: We found that neurons sending input to vH were widely dispersed throughout the entire BA, including in BLA, BMA and MEA, as well as in more cortical amygdala areas (Figure 1B–D, McDonald and Mott, 2017; Strange et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing shown in Figure 1.

claim: 3.7% of BA neurons that projected to vH were GABAergic.
source: Using this approach, we found that a small but consistent proportion of BA neurons (3.7% of CTXβ-labelled neurons) that projected to vH were GABAergic (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing in vGAT-cre mice shown in Figure 2.

claim: Inhibitory projection neurons were intermingled with excitatory projection neurons, such that there was no obvious anatomical separation between inhibitory and classic excitatory projections.
source: Using whole-brain registration as before, we found that inhibitory projection neurons were intermingled with excitatory projection neurons, such that there was no obvious anatomical separation between inhibitory and classic excitatory projections.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-brain registration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both inhibitory and excitatory projection neurons were found in consistent proportions (~4% of labelled neurons) throughout each nucleus in BA and across all three anatomical axes.
source: Supporting this, both were found in consistent proportions (~4% of labelled neurons) throughout each nucleus in BA and across all three anatomical axes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-brain registration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A proportion of CTX+ BA neurons projecting to vH were also somatostatin positive.
source: Consistent with previous results, we found that a proportion of CTX+ BA neurons projecting to vH were also somatostatin positive (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: BA input makes excitatory connections with vH pyramidal neurons via AMPA receptors.
source: By recording in voltage clamp at –70 mV, we could isolate excitatory currents in response to blue light in ~40% of recorded neurons that were blocked by bath application of the AMPA receptor antagonist NBQX (Figure 2C, paired t-test, t(8) = 10.04, p=0.000008, n = 9 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BA input makes inhibitory connections with vH pyramidal neurons via GABA-A receptors.
source: In the same neurons, we could also record inhibitory currents at 0 mV in ~30% of cells that were blocked by the GABA-A receptor antagonist gabazine (Figure 2E, paired t-test, t(8) = 11.7, p=1.48 × 10–7, n = 12 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A proportion of inhibitory input from BA to vH is due to a direct long-range inhibitory projection.
source: Interestingly, while inhibition was completely blocked in a subset of neurons (8/12), in the remaining population inhibitory currents persisted. This finding suggests that – consistent with our retrograde anatomy – a proportion of this inhibitory input was due to a direct long-range inhibitory projection from the BA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CaMKii+ BA input evoked strong inhibitory currents at 0 mV that were blocked by NBQX, showing that the inhibitory currents were a result of solely feedforward inhibition.
source: Consistent with the presence of both excitatory and inhibitory projections, CaMKii+ BA input evoked strong inhibitory currents at 0 mV (Figure 2G), but these currents were blocked by bath application of NBQX, showing that the inhibitory currents were a result of solely feedforward inhibition (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(2,4) = 23.4, p=0.006; Tukey's post hoc test, baseline vs. NBQX, t(2) = 4.73, p=0.001, baseline vs. gabazine, t(2) = 4.84, p=0.001, NBQX vs. gabazine, t(2) = 0.12, p=0.90, n = 3 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM shown in Figure 2G.

claim: vGAT+ BA input showed robust input at 0 mV that was insensitive to NBQX application, but blocked by gabazine, suggesting a direct inhibitory connection.
source: In contrast, vGAT+ BA input also showed robust input at 0 mV (Figure 2I), but this inhibitory current was insensitive to NBQX application, but blocked by gabazine, suggesting a direct inhibitory connection (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(2,10) = 10.03, p=0.004; Tukey's post hoc test, baseline vs. NBQX, t(2) = 0.05, p=0.9, baseline vs. gabazine, t(2) = 4.12, p=0.001, NBQX vs. gabazine, t(2) = 4.16, p=0.001, n = 6 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRACM shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Light-evoked excitatory BA input was on average equivalent onto both vHBA and vHNAc populations.
source: Sequential paired recordings of vHBA and vHNAc neurons showed that light-evoked excitatory BA input was on average equivalent onto both populations (Figure 4A–C, Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 15, p=0.43, n = 9 pairs of neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Paired recordings of vHBA and vHPFC neurons revealed an almost complete lack of excitatory input onto vHPFC neurons.
source: In contrast, paired recordings of vHBA and vHPFC neurons revealed an almost complete lack of excitatory input onto vHPFC neurons (Figure 4D–F, Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 0, p=0.0018, n = 8 pairs of neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Paired recordings of vHBA and vHNAc neurons showed a marked bias of inhibitory input to vHBA neurons, with consistently smaller input onto neighbouring vHNAc neurons.
source: Paired recordings of vHBA and vHNAc neurons showed a marked bias of inhibitory input to vHBA neurons, with consistently smaller input onto neighbouring vHNAc neurons (Figure 4G–I, Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 0, p=0.016, n = 7 pairs of neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: Pairs of vHBA and vHPFC projecting neurons showed essentially no connectivity from BA to vHPFC neurons.
source: Similarly to excitatory input, pairs of vHBA and vHPFC projecting neurons showed essentially no connectivity from BA to vHPFC neurons (Figure 4J–L, Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 0, p=0.016, n = 7 pairs of neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: Both inhibitory and excitatory input from BA connect with local interneurons as well as pyramidal projection neurons in vH.
source: We found similar levels of both excitatory and inhibitory connectivity to input from BA onto local interneurons as we found with pyramidal neurons (in both cases, ~50% of recorded neurons were connected). Thus, both inhibitory and excitatory input from BA connect with local interneurons as well as pyramidal projection neurons in vH.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings of interneurons shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Voltage-clamp recordings at –70 mV showed robust responses from both vHNAc and vHBA neurons onto local interneurons (~80% of recorded neurons were connected in each condition).
source: Voltage-clamp recordings at –70 mV showed robust responses from both vHNAc and vHBA neurons onto local interneurons (~80% of recorded neurons were connected in each condition, Figure 5E–H), confirming previous studies suggesting strong feedback inhibition in vH (Lee et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Local inhibitory connectivity was markedly biased towards vHNAc neurons, where inhibitory connections onto vHNAc neurons were on average twice the strength of those onto neighbouring vHBA neurons.
source: We found that local inhibitory connectivity was markedly biased towards vHNAc neurons (Figure 5I–K), where inhibitory connections onto vHNAc neurons were on average twice the strength of those onto neighbouring vHBA neurons (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 2, p=0.006, n = 10 pairs of neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 5I-K.

claim: Feedforward inhibition recorded at 0 mV was markedly biased towards vHNAc neurons.
source: In contrast, and as predicted, feedforward inhibition recorded at 0 mV was markedly biased towards vHNAc neurons (Figure 5O and P, Wilcoxon rank-sum, W = 3, p=0.04, n = 10 pairs of neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 5O-P.

claim: Increasing inhibitory input resulted in a switch in the activity of the different populations, where vHNAc neuron activity increased as direct inhibition increased, and vHBA neuron activity decreased.
source: We found that increasing inhibitory input resulted in a switch in the activity of the different populations (Figure 6B and C). While vHPFC neurons remained silent, vHNAc neuron activity increased as direct inhibition increased, and vHBA neuron activity decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 6.

claim: Long-range inhibition efficiently removes feedforward and feedback inhibition onto vHNAc neurons – both by direct inhibition of local interneuron activity, but also by inhibiting vHBA neurons that provide the bulk of feedback inhibitory drive.
source: This was due to long-range inhibition efficiently removing feedforward and feedback inhibition onto vHNAc neurons (Figure 6D) – both by direct inhibition of local interneuron activity, but also by inhibiting vHBA neurons that provide the bulk of feedback inhibitory drive.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Activation of both excitatory and inhibitory BA input supported RTPP in ChR2-expressing animals compared to GFP controls.
source: Consistent with our circuit analysis showing BA input activating vHNAc neurons, this stimulus supported RTPP in ChR2-expressing animals compared to GFP controls (t-test, t(5.9) = 2.61, p=0.041, GFP n = 6 mice, ChR2 n = 8 mice), with no change in the total distance moved during the session (Figure 7B, C and t-test, t(9.2) = 1.27, p=0.23).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetics shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Bath application of salvinorin B (SalB) hyperpolarises KORD-expressing vHNAc neurons and reduces AP firing.
source: We first tested the efficacy of KORDs expressed in vHNAc neurons and confirmed that the KORD agonist salvinorin B (SalB) hyperpolarised vHNAc neurons and resulted in a decrease in current-induced action potential firing (Figure 7D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: After injection of SalB in KORD-expressing animals, RTPP was abolished.
source: However, after injection of SalB in KORD-expressing animals, RTPP was abolished (mixed-effect ANOVA, effect of group [control vs. KORD]: F(1,14) = 15.97, p=0.001, effect of drug [SalB vs. DMSO]: F(1,14) = 15.06, p=0.002, interaction: F(1,14) = 7.45, p=0.016; post hoc paired t-test: control DSMO vs. SalB, t(8) = 1.1, p=0.3, n = 9 mice, KORD DMSO vs. SalB, t(6) = 4.62, p=0.004, n = 7 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetics combined with pharmacogenetics shown in Figure 7J-K.

claim: Excitatory BA input alone was unable to support RTPP in either GFP- or ChR2-expressing animals.
source: Consistent with the predictions from our circuit analysis, this assay showed that the light stimulus was unable to support RTPP in either GFP- or ChR2-expressing animals (Figure 8B and C and t-test, t(6.4) = 0.40, p=0.70, GFP n = 4 mice, ChR2 n = 7 mice) and was again accompanied by no change in distance travelled (t-test, t(6.9) = 0.08, p=0.94).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetics shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: Bath application of salvinorin B (SalB) hyperpolarises KORD-expressing vHBA neurons and reduces AP firing.
source: We first ensured that KORD-expressing vHBA neuron excitability was inhibited by bath application of SalB (Figure 8D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiology shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: After SalB injections in KORD-expressing animals, light stimulation supported RTPP.
source: However, after SalB injections in KORD-expressing animals, light stimulation now supported RTPP (mixed-effect ANOVA, effect of group [control vs. KORD]: F(1,14) = 3.56, p=0.08, effect of drug [SalB vs. DMSO]: F(1,14) = 3.0, p=0.11, interaction: F(1,14) = 10.85, p=0.005; post hoc paired t-test: control DSMO vs. SalB, t(8) = 1.01, p=0.34, n = 9 mice, KORD DMSO vs. SalB, t(6) = 3.14, p=0.02, n = 7 mice).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetics combined with pharmacogenetics shown in Figure 8J-K.

claim: BA provides a parallel excitatory and inhibitory projection from BA to vH that can support goal-directed behaviour.
source: Our results define a parallel excitatory and inhibitory projection from BA to vH that can support goal-directed behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined experimental data from the study.

claim: Excitatory projections from BA uniquely target vH neurons that project to NAc and back to the BA, and do not connect with neurons that project to PFC.
source: We show that excitatory projections uniquely target vH neurons that project to NAc and back to the BA, and do not connect with neurons that project to PFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Long-range inhibitory input preferentially targets BA-projecting vH neurons.
source: In contrast, long-range inhibitory input preferentially targets BA-projecting vH neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: The ability of BA input to drive motivation- and value-promoting vH projections to NAc was dependent on the co-activation of both excitatory and inhibitory input from BA.
source: Next, using a simple network model constrained by our electrophysiology recordings, we predicted that the ability of BA input to drive motivation- and value-promoting vH projections to NAc was dependent on the co-activation of both excitatory and inhibitory input from BA.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 6.

claim: Long-range inhibition is required for the generation of spatial place preference.
source: Finally, we confirmed these predictions using in vivo optogenetics and genetically targeted pharmacology to show that long-range inhibition is required for the generation of spatial place preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetics and pharmacogenetics shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Excitatory input from BA to vH can only support RTPP if accompanied by inhibition of BA-projecting vH neurons.
source: This experiment supports our hypothesis that vHNAc activity and hence RTPP is crucially dependent on the activity of both excitatory and inhibitory input from BA. Excitatory BA input to vH can only support RTPP if accompanied by inhibition of BA-projecting vH neurons, in effect mimicking the effect of BA inhibitory input on the circuit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo optogenetics combined with pharmacogenetics shown in Figure 8.

claim: Reduction in vHBA activity removes local feedback inhibition and allows excitatory BA input to drive vHNAc activity, which can support place preference.
source: Our model predicts that this reduction in vHBA activity removes local feedback inhibition (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and allows excitatory BA input to drive vHNAc activity, which can support place preference.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiple BA nuclei project to vH.
source: While the majority of investigation of BA-vH connectivity is focussed on projections specifically from the BLA, it is known that multiple BA nuclei project to vH (McDonald and Mott, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The BA inhibitory projection arose from GABAergic neurons interspersed between excitatory projection neurons throughout the entire extent of the BA.
source: We found that the BA inhibitory projection arose from GABAergic neurons interspersed between excitatory projection neurons throughout the entire extent of the BA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole-brain registration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Long-range inhibitory projections from classical excitatory projection areas have been increasingly identified as having a key role in shaping circuit output and for defining motivated behaviour.
source: Long-range inhibitory projections from classical excitatory projection areas have been increasingly identified as having a key role in shaping circuit output and for defining motivated behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature in the discussion.

claim: Functional inhibitory projections from PFC to NAc and BA to PFC have both been shown to modulate value-based and reward behaviour, including the support of RTPP and aversion.
source: For example, functional inhibitory projections from PFC to NAc (Lee et al., 2014b), and BA to PFC (Seo et al., 2016) have both been shown to modulate value-based and reward behaviour, including the support of RTPP and aversion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The hippocampus receives long-range inhibitory input from numerous regions including entorhinal, septum and PFC.
source: The hippocampus also receives long-range inhibitory input from numerous regions including entorhinal (Basu et al., 2016; Melzer et al., 2012), septum (Schlesiger et al., 2021) and PFC (Malik et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Long-range inhibition from entorhinal cortex, septum and PFC all preferentially target interneurons and avoid pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, long-range inhibition from entorhinal cortex, septum and PFC all preferentially target interneurons and avoid pyramidal neurons (Basu et al., 2016; Melzer et al., 2012; Schlesiger et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BA long-range inhibition connects with both interneurons and pyramidal neurons, similar to that seen in long-range inhibitory projections from BA to PFC.
source: In contrast, our data show that BA long-range inhibition connects with both interneurons and pyramidal neurons (Figure 4), similar to that seen in long-range inhibitory projections from BA to PFC (Seo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to prior literature.

claim: vHNAc neurons have been shown to be key for motivated behaviour, and the association of reward with a particular place or time.
source: In particular, vHNAc neurons have been shown to be key for motivated behaviour, and the association of reward with a particular place or time (Britt et al., 2012; Ciocchi et al., 2015; LeGates et al., 2018; Okuyama et al., 2016; Trouche et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Roughly 80–90% of neurons in vH are thought to project to a single downstream region.
source: While roughly 80–90 % of neurons are thought to project to a single downstream region (Figure 3, Gergues et al., 2020; Naber and Witter, 1998; Wee and MacAskill, 2020), a proportion of vH neurons collateralise and project to two or more regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to prior literature.

claim: A proportion of vH neurons collateralise and project to two or more regions.
source: While roughly 80–90 % of neurons are thought to project to a single downstream region (Figure 3, Gergues et al., 2020; Naber and Witter, 1998; Wee and MacAskill, 2020), a proportion of vH neurons collateralise and project to two or more regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to prior literature.

claim: The switch in activity from vHBA to vHNAc populations was robust despite large overlap of each projection population.
source: Importantly, however, using our circuit model we found that the switch in activity from vHBA to vHNAc populations was robust despite large overlap of each projection population (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dual-projecting neurons are much more prominent in the proximal CA1 (at the CA1/CA2 border).
source: Dual-projecting neurons are much more prominent in the proximal CA1 (at the CA1/CA2 border; Naber and Witter, 1998; Wee and MacAskill, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proximal CA1 is preferentially associated with place coding and spatial navigation.
source: This part of CA1 is preferentially associated with place coding and spatial navigation (Ciocchi et al., 2015; Henriksen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In distal CA1, dual-projection neurons are rarer.
source: In this part of the hippocampus, dual-projection neurons are rarer (Naber and Witter, 1998), and this difference in cellular properties coincides with a preferential role of distal CA1 in non-spatial and object-place associations (Igarashi et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Distal CA1 has a preferential role in non-spatial and object-place associations.
source: In this part of the hippocampus, dual-projection neurons are rarer (Naber and Witter, 1998), and this difference in cellular properties coincides with a preferential role of distal CA1 in non-spatial and object-place associations (Igarashi et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Multiple studies have examined the role of excitatory BLA input into vH in the generation of anxiety-like behaviour.
source: In addition to the role of BA and vH in value-based and motivated behaviour, multiple studies have examined the role of excitatory BLA input into vH in the generation of anxiety-like behaviour (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The vH has a key role in the generation of appropriate behaviour in anxiogenic environments.
source: The vH has a key role in the generation of appropriate behaviour in anxiogenic environments (Gray and McNaughton, 2003; Kjelstrup et al., 2002; McHugh et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vH resolves approach-avoidance conflict during decision-making via vHPFC projection neurons.
source: This is thought to be achieved both by resolving approach-avoidance conflict during decision-making via vHPFC projection neurons (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Sanchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2021), but recently also via generation of a specific anxiogenic state defined via projections to the lateral hypothalamus (LH; Jimenez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: vH generates a specific anxiogenic state via projections to the lateral hypothalamus.
source: This is thought to be achieved both by resolving approach-avoidance conflict during decision-making via vHPFC projection neurons (Padilla-Coreano et al., 2016; Sanchez-Bellot and MacAskill, 2021), but recently also via generation of a specific anxiogenic state defined via projections to the lateral hypothalamus (LH; Jimenez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BA input does innervate vHLH neurons.
source: However, BA input does innervate vHLH neurons (Gergues et al., 2020; Wee and MacAskill, 2020), and thus it is interesting to note the possibility that the anxiogenic influence of excitatory, anterior BLA input (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2020) may be via this distinct circuit.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The anxiogenic influence of excitatory, anterior BLA input may be via the vHLH circuit.
source: However, BA input does innervate vHLH neurons (Gergues et al., 2020; Wee and MacAskill, 2020), and thus it is interesting to note the possibility that the anxiogenic influence of excitatory, anterior BLA input (Felix-Ortiz et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2020) may be via this distinct circuit.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from prior literature.

claim: vHLH neurons are present in more distal areas of ventral subiculum, with only a minority present in the CA1/proximal subiculum border region.
source: vHLH neurons are present in more distal areas of ventral subiculum, with only a minority present in the CA1/proximal subiculum border region considered in this study (Wee and MacAskill, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anatomical studies have suggested that BA inhibitory projections are preferentially observed in somatostatin (SOM)- and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons.
source: Anatomical studies have suggested that BA inhibitory projections are preferentially observed in somatostatin (SOM)- and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons (McDonald et al., 2012; McDonald and Zaric, 2015), and almost completely absent in parvalbumin (PV)- and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BA inhibitory projections are almost completely absent in parvalbumin (PV)- and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing neurons.
source: Anatomical studies have suggested that BA inhibitory projections are preferentially observed in somatostatin (SOM)- and neuropeptide Y (NPY)-expressing neurons (McDonald et al., 2012; McDonald and Zaric, 2015), and almost completely absent in parvalbumin (PV)- and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is enormous diversity of interneuron types throughout the hippocampus.
source: There is enormous diversity of interneuron types throughout the hippocampus (Group et al., 2008), each of which is involved in distinct parts of the circuit calculation – such as dendritic-targeting SOM- and VIP-expressing neurons, perisomatic PV-expressing interneurons and cholecystokinin (CCK)-expressing interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitory input from entorhinal cortex preferentially innervates CCK interneurons.
source: Inhibitory input from entorhinal cortex preferentially innervates CCK interneurons (Basu et al., 2016), while input from PFC specifically innervates VIP interneurons (Malik et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Input from PFC specifically innervates VIP interneurons.
source: Inhibitory input from entorhinal cortex preferentially innervates CCK interneurons (Basu et al., 2016), while input from PFC specifically innervates VIP interneurons (Malik et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The reciprocal connection from vH to BA has been shown to undergo robust plasticity.
source: The reciprocal connection from vH to BA has been shown to undergo robust plasticity (Bazelot et al., 2015), and BA circuitry rapidly updates in response to learning cue associations (Beyeler et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2015b; Namburi et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BA circuitry rapidly updates in response to learning cue associations.
source: The reciprocal connection from vH to BA has been shown to undergo robust plasticity (Bazelot et al., 2015), and BA circuitry rapidly updates in response to learning cue associations (Beyeler et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2015b; Namburi et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: First, in the standard CRACM setup, light-evoked currents in postsynaptic neurons are heavily dependent on the number of connections with ChR2-positive axons, as well as the amplitude of the postsynaptic response at each connected synapse (MacAskill et al., 2014; MacAskill et al., 2012; Marques et al., 2018; Petreanu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.
